newsitem.title: USA: Gold seen retaining key world monetary role - WGC.
newsitem.headline: Gold seen retaining key world monetary role - WGC.

text.p: Despite recent European central bank gold sales ahead of the planned introduction of the single European currency in 1999, many central bankers still believe gold has a key role to play in the world's monetary system, said Robert Pringle, head of World Gold Council's (WGC) Center for Public Policy Studies.

"Assuming EMU (European monetary union) will happen, the general view among central bankers is that gold will probably play much the same role as it does now - it will still be the bedrock of the reserve asset structure," Pringle told Gold and Silver Institute annual conference here.
"But although gold is likely to be part of the pooled external reserve assets of the ECB (European central bank), we do not yet know how big a part," he added.

"The Banque de France takes the view that gold reserves are one of the elements underpinning confidence in the currency, and some countries will try to retain control over a large part of their gold reserves as an ultimate safeguard against the possible breakdown of EMU or of the whole system," he said.

"The introduction of the euro will cause the biggest shake- up in reserve currencies since sterling handed over its dominant role to the dollar 50 years ago, so although it is natural to expect further gold sales by some central banks, it will be equally natural to expect other official holders to be interested in increasing their gold holdings," he said.
European central banks hold about 14,300 tonnes of gold (460 million ounces), or more than 40 percent of all official world gold reserves.
World central banks are believed to hold about 36,000 tonnes of gold, about a quarter of the world's estimated above- ground stocks of 129,000 tonnes at the end of 1995.

Earlier this month, after heavy political pressure, Switzerland moved to set up a $4.7 billion fund to compensate Holocaust victims, financed by revaluing gold reserves held by the Swiss National Bank.

If approved in a referendum next year, the plan will result in revalued gold -- worth seven billion Swiss francs or about 440 tonnes -- being transferred to the new fund which is expected to sell it over a ten year period and invest the proceeds in interest bearing securities.

The amount of gold sales involved over such a period is less than Canada's sales program of the last 15 years and will be small relative to the world's annual supply of gold of over 3,000 tonnes, Pringle said.
And "the use of their gold reserves in this fashion should not be construed as an indication that they now suddenly hold gold in less regard," he said.
"Notably, Swiss bank notes will still enjoy a 100 percent coverage of gold when valued at the market," he said.
The Swiss constitution requires the Swiss central bank to hold gold reserves equal to 40 percent of the currency in circulation.
"In fact the proposal confirms gold's reserve attributes as a highly liquid store of value that can be readily called upon in times of national need," Pringle said.

Despite the publicity about the 500 tonnes of gold sold by the Belgian and Dutch central bank sales last year, central bank gold sales since 1989 have reduced official holdings by less than five percent, he argued.
"The overall picture is one of massive stability - official sector holdings have been about 33,000-35,000 tonnes for nearly 30 years," he said.
And some of the net reduction in official holdings since 1989 may have been acquired by government agencies in Asia without showing up in official statistics, he said.
"We know that the monetary authorities in Singapore and Hong Kong hold gold, but we do not know how much."
"There probably will be a further flow of gold out of European central banks and there probably will be further purchases by others," he said.
Currently, Asian developing countries have only about six percent of world gold reserves but 28 pct of world foreign currency reserves, he noted.
-Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 1-212-859-1641
